brief.head: Bad bankers
brief.text: Finance means processing information, forecasting and taking risks, Ajay Shah said, and bureaucrats have no incentive to do it. State meddling in finance is “a dismal mess”. {109-C07}

brief.head: The 99 per cent
brief.text: Lant Pritchett found that human welfare indicators correlate around 99 per cent with per capita GDP, Amit Varma said. Redistribution and welfarism are left the remaining one per cent. {109-R08}

brief.head: Training the gut
brief.text: Woken at 3 a.m., Ajay Shah said, his mind runs on the price system and general equilibrium. Intuitions can be retrained, Amit Varma said, by “light bulb moments”. {109-C03}

brief.head: Credit means debt
brief.text: Restate a claim from the other side, Amit Varma said, quoting Henry Hazlitt: more credit means more debt, subsidies mean higher taxes, more exports ultimately mean more imports. {109-C16}

brief.head: Mind the individual
brief.text: Think of real people, not abstractions such as the nation, Amit Varma said: Hazlitt traced many fallacies to forgetting “the individuals who make it up and give it meaning”. {109-C17}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah read Henry Hazlitt’s classic
lead.head: A 1946 lesson, still unlearnt
body: Henry Hazlitt published *Economics in One Lesson* in 1946. In later editions, Amit Varma said, he added chapters but did not change a word of the original text, because its principles still held.
It was the first of a planned series in which the hosts take apart one book at a time, and Varma said its fallacies are still being committed today.
He read out Hazlitt’s own diagnosis from 1946: “This book is an analysis of economic fallacies that are at last so prevalent that they have become almost a new orthodoxy.”
They survive, Varma said, because economics’ deepest truths are counterintuitive. Intuition says the world is zero-sum and must be run from the top down.
## The art of economics

The lesson of the title fits in two sentences, which Varma read aloud: “The art of economics consists in looking not merely at the immediate but at the longer effects of any act or policy. It consists in tracing the consequences of that policy not merely for one group, but for all groups.” {109-C01}
Hazlitt took the method from the essayist Frédéric Bastiat, whose parable of the broken window is a lesson in what goes unseen.

A boy breaks a shop window, and a bystander calls it good for the economy, because the glazier gets paid. Unseen is what the shopkeeper would have spent the money on instead: a suit, and through it the tailor.
That, Varma said, is opportunity cost. The same logic disposes of the claim that war is good for the economy.
## The unseen bill
The rest of the book applies the lesson chapter by chapter. Public works mean taxes: for every public job a bridge creates, a private job is destroyed somewhere else.

Taxes discourage production, and Varma translated them into time: “If you are taxed one third of your income, that means that for four months of the year you are working for the government of India, you’re not working for yourself.” {109-C06}

The fear that machines destroy jobs has recurred from the Luddites to today’s worries about AI. Varma had no patience for it: “There’s never been an exception, and there is no reason to believe there will be an exception this time.” {109-C08}
Ajay Shah added that a society can only consume what it produces, and that new technology spreads slowly, leaving time to adjust.
## Rent and compassion
The hosts saved their longest argument for rent control, a chapter Hazlitt added in 1961.
Price controls always cause scarcity, Varma said. Marine Drive in Bombay has sprawling flats let for a few hundred rupees a month, in dilapidated buildings nobody maintains. {109-C13}

The subject is back in the news. Zohran Mamdani, who won New York’s Democratic mayoral primary, wants rent control. Varma found him charming and his economic policies “a throwback to the worst excesses of the twentieth century”.
Such schemes let people project virtue, Varma argued. True compassion asks whether a policy helps the people it means to help, and these, he said, hurt the poor.

Varma’s guiding framework, he said, Adam Smith had stated long before him: what is prudence in a family can scarcely be folly in a kingdom. “All decent people, in our personal dealings, we are libertarian,” Varma said. The task is to carry those values over to the state. {109-C20}

second.label: Depression economics
second.head: Autobahns to recovery
second.deck: Ajay Shah finds one exception to Henry Hazlitt’s case against make-work spending
body: Ajay Shah broadly agrees with Henry Hazlitt that make-work spending is a mistake. He made one exception: the Great Depression.

Mistakes in monetary policy had collapsed the money supply, and a quarter of all banks went bust. Firms that lost their bank could not easily start again with another. Adolf Hitler then borrowed to rearm and build autobahns, and the jobs and re-spending pulled Germany out of the slump, Shah said. {109-S03}

Amit Varma replied that Hazlitt’s target was governments that build what is not needed “under the guise of producing employment”. {#guise} On the Depression, he pointed to contrary accounts by Amity Shlaes and Thomas Sowell.

quote.text: He actually wanted the arms, he actually wanted the autobahns.

second.caption: the Great Depression exception

third.head: Painting by numbers
body: Amit Varma had a quiz for Ajay Shah. He showed him a painting by the artist Tatsuo Horiuchi and asked what medium it was made in. Shah had no idea. {109-S07}
“He made it using a technology you referred to five minutes ago,” Varma said. “He made it using Microsoft Excel.”

Shah had just been arguing that new technologies spread slowly. Spreadsheets existed by the mid-1970s, he said, yet large parts of Indian business still lack even basic spreadsheet skills. {#spreadsheets}

Varma had introduced the quiz with Arthur C. Clarke’s line that any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic. The word defeated him. It came out as “internationalization from magic”. {109-J11} A spreadsheet, it turned out, could also be a paintbrush.
third.caption: the painting made in Excel

p2.title: Hazlitt, applied
p2.deck: Henry Hazlitt’s *Economics in One Lesson*, chapter by chapter, as Amit Varma and Ajay Shah took it apart

sections.label: The book
sections.head: Lights you can’t switch off
sections.caption: why the book still matters
body: Every five episodes or so, Amit Varma announced, the hosts will pick one book that shaped them and break it down. He began with Henry Hazlitt’s *Economics in One Lesson*. {#everyfive}

The book came out in 1946 and was an immediate bestseller. Hazlitt added a chapter on rent control in 1961, expanded it in 1978 and added a closing chapter, but left the rest untouched. Fundamental principles, Varma said, need little updating, as in physics.

Such books are needed because economics’ deepest truths, such as spontaneous order and positive-sum exchange, run against intuition. Intuition tells us the world is zero-sum and must be controlled from the top down. Varma noticed Ajay Shah smiling: “Because you are the man on the top controlling.” {109-J04}
## Seeing order everywhere
Intuitions can be retrained, Varma argued, through light bulb moments that cannot be undone. {109-C03} His came from Friedrich Hayek’s essay *The Use of Knowledge in Society*, on how prices work.
Matt Ridley’s *The Evolution of Everything* showed him spontaneous order running through natural selection, language and prices. “It is so miraculous,” he said. {109-R11}
~ The hosts, Varma said, try to throw light bulbs at the screen. Shah promptly imagined the merchandise: a cannon beside the TV, firing defunct tungsten bulbs at the viewer on Varma’s cue. {109-J05}

quote.text: You flick a switch and the light comes on. And you can never unsee what you have just seen.

sections.label: The parable
sections.head: The suit nobody saw
sections.caption: the broken window
body: Henry Hazlitt’s lesson sets two economists side by side. “The bad economist sees only what immediately strikes the eye. The good economist also looks beyond,” Amit Varma read. {109-C01}

Hazlitt also mocked an unnamed economist who said that in the long run we are all dead. Ajay Shah guessed at once: “I love John Maynard Keynes dearly and one of his crimes was that he was wise, witty, and wonderful.” {109-J03}
## A window and a war

Hazlitt drew on Frédéric Bastiat’s parable. A boy breaks a shop window, and a bystander, in Varma’s telling “no doubt a wise Bengali economist”, hails the glazier’s windfall as a stimulus. {109-J06} Varma, a Bengali himself, later said he does not like Bengali economists either.

The unseen half is the suit the shopkeeper would have bought, and the tailor who would have spent the money in turn. {109-C02} That is opportunity cost, and the same logic sinks the claim that war, or rebuilding ruined cities, is good for the economy.
~ For Shah, the biggest example is growth against redistribution. Redistribution, he said, pits people against people: “This is a game of class warfare.” {109-C04}

quote.text: What is not seen is what the shopkeeper would have done with the twenty rupees had he kept it with himself.

sections.label: The taxman
sections.head: Where bridges can be built
sections.caption: bridges, taxes and time
body: Nothing the government does is free, Amit Varma said: it is paid for in taxes, and so through coercion. Henry Hazlitt’s chapter on public works shows the trade. “For every public job created by the bridge project, a private job has been destroyed somewhere else.” {109-C05}
Once jobs become the goal, Hazlitt wrote, governments stop asking where bridges must be built and ask where they can be built. Varma sees the same make-work logic in India’s NREGS.
## Months for the state

Taxes also discourage production. Varma urged listeners to count their taxes in months of work. {109-C06} Everyone pays, he said: the beggar at the traffic signal buying salt, the domestic help buying soap. Inflation is a tax on the poor.
Under Indira Gandhi, he recalled, the peak personal income tax rate was 95 or 97 per cent, an incentive to leave the country or to hoard black money. {#peakrate}

~ Varma called India’s space programme a waste of money. Ajay Shah, tongue in cheek, called it real progress that India paid a foreign company to launch an Indian astronaut: cheaper, with the same propaganda value. Carried to its logical conclusion, he said, “what you need is an AI video”. {109-J07}

sections.label: The machine
sections.head: Chicken in, cars out
sections.caption: machines, trade and jobs
body: Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it, George Santayana wrote, and Amit Varma is tired of each new wave of technophobia, from the Luddites to today’s fears about AI. {109-J15}

Henry Hazlitt’s answer starts with Adam Smith’s pin-makers. A workman with machinery could make 4,800 pins a day where one without could scarcely make one, yet employment went up, not down. If saving labour were bad, Hazlitt asked, why not carry freight on men’s backs?
## Magic at the port

Ajay Shah’s rebuttal was that society’s aggregate consumption is its aggregate production, so productivity gains raise consumption per head. {109-C09} And adoption is slow. Driverless cars will replace India’s drivers, he said, but over probably 25 years. {#driverless}

Trade, he added, is a technology too. Frozen chicken from Maharashtra’s poultry farms leaves JNPT and comes back as electric vehicles, a rival to Mahindra’s factory at Igatpuri. {109-C10} To stop progress, you would have to shut down trade as well.
~ What turns change into conflict is culture, Shah argued. Great societies are “more Gandhiji and less Karl Marx”. {109-C11}

quote.text: So sitting at JNPT is a piece of magic that converts frozen chicken into electric vehicles.

sections.label: The landlord
sections.head: Rent frozen, capital dead
sections.caption: rent control and dead capital
body: Rent control is back in the news. Zohran Mamdani, winner of New York’s Democratic mayoral primary and son of Mira Nair, one of Amit Varma’s favourite filmmakers, wants it. Varma finds him charming, condemns the racist attacks on him and calls his policies “a throwback to the worst excesses of the twentieth century”. {109-J20}

The seen effect is that tenants are spared rising rents. The unseen effects, Varma said, are that landlords stop maintaining buildings, developers stop building, and tenants stop economising on space. {109-C13}
## Dead capital

Varma borrowed a concept from Hernando de Soto’s *The Mystery of Capital*: without title, land that people effectively own cannot be borrowed against, so it is dead capital. {109-R26} Rent control, he argued, turns living property into dead capital: “It is equal to theft.”

Opponents of such schemes, Varma said, are made to sound evil. A tweet by Daniel Hannan reminded him of a leftist friend who once told him: “Amit, I didn’t realise you cared so much. I thought you’re libertarian, you don’t give a shit about people.” {109-S06}
~ Ajay Shah offered Mamdani the old line about communism, the heart and the brain: “So give him a break.” Varma’s reply: “Thirty-four is old enough.” {109-J12}

quote.text: You have taken an apartment or a building or a building block or a neighborhood and you made it dead capital.

sections.label: The toolkit
sections.head: Five lenses for any policy
sections.caption: the Hazlitt toolkit
body: Amit Varma drew three broad lessons from the book. Look at longer effects and at all groups. Think of individuals, not abstractions such as the nation. {109-C17} And restate every claim from the other side.

Then came a toolkit: opportunity cost, general welfare over interest groups, incentives and distortions, the price system, and capital formation. The price system, Varma said, should be treated as sacred. {109-C19}
## Who pays, who gains

From his friend Suyash Rai, Varma took a warning about cost-benefit sums. The cost falls on one group now, the benefit on another, often imagined and in the future. Demonetisation, he said, had no benefits at all. {109-C18}

His most important framework, Varma said, was one Adam Smith had stated long before him: what is prudence in a family can scarcely be folly in a kingdom. Friends at a restaurant do not force each other to eat or to pay, he said, yet coercion seems fine one level up, at the state. {109-C20}

~ Ajay Shah urged listeners to read the book itself: Varma telling its story, he said, was “one hundredth of reading the book”. {#hundredth} Asked about young Ajays running around the world, Shah said they would soon get over the delusion “that there is anything here which is somehow special”. “Oh my god, such modesty,” said Varma.

quote.text: Prices are how we get information about what others can do for us and what we could possibly do for them.

side.boxText: Lant Pritchett told Amit Varma this was the book that turned him onto economics. Henry Hazlitt, “a great essayist and thinker”, published it in 1946 and, through two later editions, never changed a word of the original chapters. {109-R01}

contQuote.text: And therefore the truly compassionate people are those who think of the outcomes and they ask the question that are you actually helping the people you’re trying to help or are you hurting them?

p3.title: Tales of the unseen
p3.deck: A bureaucrat, a father, a satellite and a forest, and what each teaches

stories.end: that the universe wanted more jute and Bengali pride is now all over
stories.caption: the jute bureaucrat
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a bureaucrat, a pun and a twist
stories.head: The industry that saved itself
body: Some years ago, Amit Varma got talking to a senior bureaucrat in a West Bengal ministry. At the time, the man was looking after the jute industry.
Varma asked him what the thinking was. The jute industry was not doing well. It was an indigenous industry, “our thing”, and the government had to keep it alive.
The bureaucrat’s technocratic mind, as Varma put it, was full of subsidies, price controls and grants of land.

“And I was like, Why? Why does the government have a role to play in it?” Varma recalled. {109-S04} Let supply and demand decide, he argued. Whatever is done for jute comes at the cost of something else, and nobody sees the jobs and welfare lost there.
Midway through the retelling, Varma slipped in a Hindi pun on jute and jhoot, a lie, and refused to explain it. Ajay Shah got it “forty-five milliseconds later”, by his own count. {109-J09}

This is what Henry Hazlitt called saving the X industry. Varma said such thinking has faded in the West but persists in India. Shah added that China runs the same playbook, “just done 5x more extreme than India”. {#china}
Then Shah delivered the twist. Jute, he said, is now doing extremely well, because global technological forces made the world want more of it, and that has nothing to do with the government. {#jute}
~ Varma had not expected that. It was, he said, “one more thing to be proud of”.
stories.why: Any favour to one industry is paid for by others, whose lost jobs go unseen. {109-C12} The punchline: jute thrived because the wider world wanted it, not because anyone saved it.
stories.postscript: The fixation got Varma’s goat, he said, adding: “I should be careful about what I say because I don’t have a goat.”

stories.caption: his father’s Bombay
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on his father’s Bombay, before rent control
stories.head: A flat in fifteen minutes
body: Around 1976, when Ajay Shah was about ten, his family of six would sit at the dinner table and talk for hours about the world. Bombay was in the throes of rent control, and renting anything was essentially impossible.

One evening his father told them about arriving in the city in 1942, the year Gandhiji launched the Quit India movement. “When I first came to Bombay, you could just walk around the street and within fifteen minutes you could rent a flat.” {109-S02}
The children were wide-eyed. To kids like them, Shah said, renting a house easily was an unbelievable concept.
~ Rent control had ended a free market. Nobody wanted to let out property, and by the 1970s the old ease had vanished. Today, Shah said, modern legal engineering makes renting far more feasible.
stories.why: Rent control’s deepest damage is invisible to those born after it. A generation can grow up thinking a broken housing market is normal, in a city where renting was once easy. It has been a disaster, Amit Varma said, wherever it has been tried. {#disaster}

stories.start: our good friend Baron Mitra had uh did this experiment with tribals in Gujarat
stories.end: my land, everything changes. The way you look at the world changes
stories.caption: Barun Mitra’s satellites
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Barun Mitra’s campaign for tribal land
stories.head: From Google Earth to pakka homes
body: About twenty years ago, Amit Varma said, the hosts’ friend Barun Mitra joined a movement in Gujarat to win property rights for tribals. The challenge was proof: how long they had lived there, and where the boundaries lay.
The answer came from space. Using historical Google Earth satellite imagery, the campaigners showed how long the tribals had been on the land, and the tribals got their rights.

“And the first thing they did, when they got the rights, was made pakka housing for themselves. They built toilets for themselves,” Varma said. {109-S05} In the past they had not, because they could be pushed out at any time.
~ The story is told in *India Awakes*, a documentary presented by Johan Norberg. {109-R30}
stories.why: Ownership changes incentives overnight. People do not invest in land they could lose, and once it is theirs, they build. It is the cure for what Hernando de Soto calls dead capital. {109-R26}

stories.start: Um I in recent weeks I spent some days in beer
stories.end: If you puke on a forest but nobody sees it, did you puke
stories.caption: the paragliding ride
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s holiday, told at his own expense
stories.head: What goes up over Bir
body: Ajay Shah opened the episode insisting he had nothing as exciting as Amit Varma’s secret project to report. Then he described a few days in Bir.
There he spent time with the trail runner Sanat Sachdev, “just all round cool person”, who got him thinking about running in the mountains. He also took a two-hour tandem paragliding ride.
At the highest point the ride turned rocky. “The guy behind me, the pilot, gently instructed me on how to stick my head out and puke on the forest below,” Shah said. {109-S01}
~ “Are you the first economist to puke on a forest?” Varma asked. {109-J02} Shah shrugged it off: anybody who does serious paragliding faces motion sickness.

quote.text: If you puke on a forest but nobody sees it, did you puke?

quiz.q: In Bastiat’s parable, what might the shopkeeper have bought with the money spent on his window?
quiz.a: A suit, so the tailor, not the glazier, would have got the money.

quiz.q: Hazlitt mocked an economist who said “In the long run we are all dead”. Whom did Ajay Shah name?
quiz.a: John Maynard Keynes, whom Shah loves dearly, crimes and all.

quiz.q: Taxed a third of your income, how much of the year are you working for the government?
quiz.a: Four months of every year, which Amit Varma called part-time slavery.

quiz.q: Where does Ajay Shah locate the “piece of magic” that turns frozen chicken into electric vehicles?
quiz.a: At JNPT, the Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust: trade, he says, is a technology.

quiz.q: What medium did the artist Tatsuo Horiuchi use for the painting Amit Varma showed Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: Microsoft Excel, the very spreadsheet technology Shah had mentioned five minutes earlier.

quiz.q: What did Gujarat’s tribals build first after winning rights to their land with satellite evidence?
quiz.a: Pakka houses and toilets, which they never built while they could be evicted.
